Name: NIST NVD
SDKs & notable repos: The curated, scored view of every CVE; JSON 2.0 is the current feed format
Downloadable / offline docs: Vulnerability data feeds as JSON from https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/data-feeds; full API, free key available
Notes: NVD is CVE plus enrichment (CWE mapping, CVSS, CPE ranges). Its enrichment has had real backlogs, so tooling that assumed NVD analysis is current has had to learn to read CVE records directly — know which layer you are consuming.

Name: CVE Program
SDKs & notable repos: CVE IDs are issued by CNAs and reserved/published through CVE Services; the record list itself is a git repository
Downloadable / offline docs: The CVE List is cloneable from the cvelist repo; bulk downloads from cve.org
Notes: The authoritative registry — cve.org is the program site, individual records live at cve.org/CVERecord. NVD adds the analysis layer on top.

Name: CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration)
Downloadable / offline docs: The full list as XML/CSV/HTML from the site's data pages
Notes: The taxonomy of software weaknesses — what NVD maps findings to and what SAST tools classify against. cwe.mitre.org 403s some automated clients; fine in a browser.

Name: CAPEC (Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification)
Downloadable / offline docs: Attack-pattern library as XML/CSV from the site's data pages
Notes: CWE describes the weakness; CAPEC describes how attackers exploit it. Read them as two halves of one vocabulary.

Name: OWASP
SDKs & notable repos: Hundreds of community projects; the Top 10 lists and the Cheat Sheet Series are the two most-cited artefacts
Downloadable / offline docs: Everything is versioned in the org's repos; project pages export to PDF
Notes: A foundation, not a product. Quality varies by project; the Cheat Sheet Series is the consistently excellent part.

Name: OWASP ASVS
SDKs & notable repos: The standard for verifying application security — levels 1-3, per-control requirements
Downloadable / offline docs: The standard as PDF plus machine-readable checklists from the project page
Notes: The document you attach to a vendor contract. ASVS turns 'is it secure?' into a numbered checklist someone can be held to.

Name: OWASP WSTG
SDKs & notable repos: The standard methodology for testing web applications, test by test
Downloadable / offline docs: PDF/EPUB built from the project repo
Notes: If a pentest report's methodology section references anything, it is this. Read the stable version.

Name: CIS Controls & Benchmarks
Downloadable / offline docs: CIS Benchmarks (per-product hardening guides) as PDFs with free registration from https://www.cisecurity.org/cis-benchmarks/
Notes: The Controls are the 18 things to do first; the Benchmarks are how to configure each specific product. Nearly every compliance conversation starts here.

Name: MITRE ATT&CK
SDKs & notable repos: The tactics/techniques matrix; the ATT&CK Navigator is the standard browsing layer
Downloadable / offline docs: STIX/JSON bundles of the full matrix from the data repo
Notes: The shared vocabulary for adversary behaviour. Detection engineering starts when your alert names match technique IDs.

Name: CISA KEV
Downloadable / offline docs: The catalog as JSON/CSV feeds from the same page
Notes: CVSS says 'severe'; KEV says 'someone is using it'. It is the only vulnerability list that should directly drive your patch SLA.

Name: AFL++
SDKs & notable repos: Coverage-guided file fuzzer; instrumentation via compiler plugins (afl-clang-fast); persistent mode
Downloadable / offline docs: Clone and build; the in-repo docs/ directory is the manual
Notes: The maintained fork of AFL and still the first tool to reach for. Read docs/README.md top to bottom; it is a fuzzing education in itself.

Name: libFuzzer
SDKs & notable repos: In-process, coverage-guided fuzzing engine that ships with clang — no separate install
Downloadable / offline docs: Ships with the compiler toolchain
Notes: Pairs with sanitizer builds (-fsanitize=fuzzer,address). The in-process model is what makes it fast — and what makes one crash kill the whole run.

Name: honggfuzz
SDKs & notable repos: Feedback-driven fuzzer with hardware-performance-counter feedback
Downloadable / offline docs: Clone and build
Notes: Development has slowed; AFL++ and libFuzzer see more use. Still worth reading for its hardware-feedback approach.

Name: OSS-Fuzz
SDKs & notable repos: Free continuous fuzzing for open-source projects; AFL++, libFuzzer and honggfuzz under the hood
Downloadable / offline docs: Docker-based local reproduction; build scripts in-repo
Notes: Thousands of projects, public corpora and bug statistics. Reading a project's OSS-Fuzz integration shows you what real fuzz targets look like.

Name: Fuzzilli
SDKs & notable repos: Coverage-guided JavaScript engine fuzzer built on a custom IR (FuzzIL)
Downloadable / offline docs: Clone and build; Swift toolchain required
Notes: Found dozens of JIT and interpreter bugs in V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore. The design write-ups explain why naive JS fuzzing fails.

Name: Jazzer
SDKs & notable repos: libFuzzer for the JVM; fuzz targets are ordinary Java methods; runs in OSS-Fuzz
Downloadable / offline docs: Maven/Gradle artifact; Bazel rules
Notes: The reason most Java projects take fuzzing seriously. Hook-based coverage, so you do not instrument bytecode by hand.

Name: Atheris
SDKs & notable repos: Fuzzing for Python; covers native extensions via sanitizer instrumentation
Downloadable / offline docs: pip-installable
Notes: Catches both Python-level exception bugs and memory corruption in C extensions — the latter is the actual reason to run it.

Name: cargo-fuzz
SDKs & notable repos: libFuzzer driver for Rust; cargo fuzz init/add/run manages targets, corpus and artifacts
Downloadable / offline docs: cargo-installable
Notes: Aim it at unsafe blocks and parsers. Even a memory-safe language needs fuzzing at every FFI boundary.

Name: GitHub CodeQL
SDKs & notable repos: Queries are logic programs over a relational database of your code; the ql/ tree is a library of vulnerability classes
Downloadable / offline docs: CLI free for research and open source; query packs distributed via the GitHub registry
Notes: Read a query for a CVE class you already know and you will understand the vulnerability better than most write-ups manage.

Name: Semgrep
SDKs & notable repos: Pattern-based SAST whose rules are short enough to read on the spot; community rules registry
Downloadable / offline docs: pip/brew-installable CLI; runs offline
Notes: The lowest-friction way to write your own organizational rules. Start with --config auto, then replace it with rules you actually own.

Name: Bandit
SDKs & notable repos: AST-based security linter for Python
Downloadable / offline docs: pip-installable
Notes: Modest but honest. Its findings list doubles as a syllabus of Python-specific footguns.

Name: Brakeman
SDKs & notable repos: Static analysis purpose-built for Rails; does not need to boot the application
Downloadable / offline docs: gem-installable
Notes: One of the few SAST tools tuned to a single framework's idioms, and better for it.

Name: FindSecBugs
SDKs & notable repos: SpotBugs plugin doing taint analysis over Java bytecode; 100+ detector types
Downloadable / offline docs: Maven/Gradle plugin
Notes: The default answer for Java SAST before CodeQL; still the easiest to wire into an existing build.

Name: Gitleaks
SDKs & notable repos: Secret scanner for git history, working trees and streams; TOML rule format
Downloadable / offline docs: Single static binary
Notes: Put it in pre-receive hooks and CI. Rotating a leaked credential costs more than every scanner on this page combined.

Name: TruffleHog
SDKs & notable repos: 800+ credential detectors, most of which verify whether the secret still works
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; Docker image
Notes: Verification is the differentiator — a 'possible key' you can confirm valid is a different incident entirely.

Name: Trivy
SDKs & notable repos: One scanner for container images, filesystems, git repos, IaC and secrets; SBOM generation built in
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; offline vulnerability DB download supported
Notes: The pragmatic default: one tool, trivy image/fs/config, done. Depth varies by ecosystem; breadth is unmatched.

Name: Grype & Syft
SDKs & notable repos: Syft (github.com/anchore/syft) builds the SBOM; Grype matches it against vulnerability feeds
Downloadable / offline docs: Single static binaries for both
Notes: The SBOM-first pipeline in two commands: syft then grype. Understanding why the two are separate teaches you what an SBOM actually is.

Name: OSV-Scanner
SDKs & notable repos: Queries the OSV database (osv.dev) with lockfile-aware version resolution
Downloadable / offline docs: Binary releases; the OSV API and data dumps are free
Notes: Resolves transitive dependencies instead of pattern-matching filenames, which is where most other scanners quietly go wrong.

Name: Dependency-Track
SDKs & notable repos: OWASP project; consumes CycloneDX SBOMs continuously and tracks risk over time
Downloadable / offline docs: Docker deployment; REST API
Notes: This is the 'keep the inventory current' half of SCA. One-off scans are trivia; a tracked SBOM is a capability.

Name: Sigstore
SDKs & notable repos: Keyless signing backed by Fulcio (certificate authority) and Rekor (transparency log); adopted by npm, PyPI and GitHub
Downloadable / offline docs: CLI clients per platform
Notes: The bet: certificates short-lived like TLS, identities tied to OIDC, everything logged publicly. Read the trust specification, not just the README.

Name: cosign
SDKs & notable repos: cosign sign / cosign verify for containers and blobs; integrates with Kubernetes admission
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary
Notes: cosign verify in an admission controller is the shortest path from supply-chain theory to enforcement.

Name: in-toto
SDKs & notable repos: Signed attestations about each step of a software pipeline; the layout file is the policy
Downloadable / offline docs: Python reference implementation; SLSA generators reuse the spec
Notes: 'Who ran what, on which input, producing which artifact' — answered cryptographically instead of by trusting CI folklore.

Name: SLSA
SDKs & notable repos: Build-platform requirements in levels; provenance-generating GitHub Actions
Downloadable / offline docs: The specification is a static site, freely readable
Notes: The framework for answering 'did this artifact come from where it claims?'. Start at the threat-model page; the levels only make sense after it.

Name: TUF (The Update Framework)
SDKs & notable repos: Metadata format and reference implementation; the specification lives at theupdateframework.io/specification
Downloadable / offline docs: Specification on the site; reference implementation in-repo
Notes: Designed against key compromise, rollback and freeze attacks. Update systems you build in an afternoon have none of these properties; TUF is the checklist.

Name: Notation (Notary Project)
SDKs & notable repos: notation sign/verify for OCI artifacts; plugin model for key stores (KMS, HSM)
Downloadable / offline docs: CLI releases
Notes: The Notary-v2 lineage that became the OCI signing approach most registries now implement. The alternative to Sigstore when you want key-based, not keyless.

Name: SPIFFE / SPIRE
SDKs & notable repos: Workload identity via SVIDs (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents); SPIRE is the reference node/workload-attestation runtime
Downloadable / offline docs: The specification documents are static and freely readable
Notes: The zero-trust answer to service credentials: no shared secrets, identities attested from the platform up. mTLS with actual attestation behind it.

Name: OpenSSF Scorecard
SDKs & notable repos: Automated supply-chain posture checks on a repository (branch protection, pinned dependencies, token permissions); public results for major projects
Downloadable / offline docs: Runs locally against any repo
Notes: The checks list doubles as a review checklist for your own repositories — that alone is worth the install.

Name: OWASP ZAP
SDKs & notable repos: Interception proxy + active scanner; scriptable via the ZAP API; add-on marketplace
Downloadable / offline docs: Desktop releases; Docker images for CI scanning
Notes: The free DAST that runs in CI. Slower and noisier than Burp's scanner; infinitely cheaper and scriptable.

Name: Burp Suite Community
Downloadable / offline docs: Free Community Edition download from the site
Notes: Community lacks the automated scanner; the proxy, Repeater and the act of reading raw requests are the actual education. The Pro edition is what professionals run at work.

Name: PortSwigger Web Security Academy
Downloadable / offline docs: All materials free; labs run in hosted environments
Notes: The best free hands-on web security curriculum in existence, maintained by the Burp vendors. If you only use one resource on this page, use this one.

Name: Nuclei
SDKs & notable repos: Template-driven scanner; thousands of community templates in nuclei-templates
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; templates update via the project's tooling
Notes: YAML templates make 'check for this specific CVE' a file you can diff and review. That reviewability is the whole point.

Name: ffuf
SDKs & notable repos: Fast web fuzzer for directories, parameters, headers and virtual hosts
Downloadable / offline docs: Single Go binary
Notes: The successor to dirb/gobuster in most toolkits. Learning to filter on response size and status is the actual skill.

Name: sqlmap
SDKs & notable repos: Automated SQL injection detection and exploitation; supports every mainstream DBMS
Downloadable / offline docs: Clone or download a release; Python
Notes: Ancient-looking, still effective, and unforgiving of careless use — it fires real payloads. Authorized targets only.

Name: JWT (jwt.io)
SDKs & notable repos: The spec is RFC 7519; jwt.io maintains the library index and the famous debugger
Notes: The classic vulnerabilities (alg: none, algorithm confusion, kid injection) are library and integration bugs. Pick a maintained library and pin the expected algorithm server-side.

Name: OWASP API Security Top 10
SDKs & notable repos: BOLA, broken authentication, SSRF and friends, ranked for API-shaped systems
Downloadable / offline docs: PDF and JSON from the project page
Notes: Read alongside the OWASP Top 10, not instead of it — APIs fail differently, and BOLA is the classic one the Web Top 10 undersells.

Name: Nmap
SDKs & notable repos: NSE scripting engine with hundreds of bundled scripts; Zenmap GUI
Downloadable / offline docs: The official book is free online; installers for every platform
Notes: Scanning well is a skill: timing templates, scan types and NSE. The free book is genuinely good.

Name: tcpdump
SDKs & notable repos: libpcap's reference consumer; its filter syntax is the one every downstream tool copies
Downloadable / offline docs: Man page and FAQ on the site; present on every Unix
Notes: The lingua franca of packet capture. If you can write tcpdump -i any 'tcp port 443' from memory, Wireshark displays become trivial.

Name: CrowdSec
SDKs & notable repos: Log-analysis agent + remediation components; crowdsourced blocklist signals
Downloadable / offline docs: Packages and Docker images; a hub of parser/scenario collections
Notes: fail2ban's modern sibling: local decisions plus shared reputation. Reading its scenarios teaches detection-as-code.

Name: fail2ban
SDKs & notable repos: Log-watching daemon that bans IPs via firewall rules; Python
Downloadable / offline docs: Packaged in every distribution
Notes: Still the default on every VPS for a reason. The jail/filter model is crude, transparent and easy to reason about.

Name: OpenSCAP
SDKs & notable repos: The oscap CLI evaluating XCCDF/OVAL content; SCAP Workbench GUI
Downloadable / offline docs: Ships in RHEL/Fedora; content packages per platform
Notes: The bridge between CIS/STIG hardening PDFs and machine-checkable reality. Evaluate, remediate, then generate the report auditors want.

Name: Wazuh
SDKs & notable repos: Open-source SIEM/XDR on OpenSearch; agents for every OS; FIM, vulnerability detection, log triage
Downloadable / offline docs: All-in-one Docker deployment; OVA image
Notes: The free baseline for 'we need a SIEM'. Noisy out of the box — tuning it is the actual exercise.

Name: osquery
SDKs & notable repos: SQL over your operating system — processes, sockets, packages and users as tables; Fleet (fleetdm.com) for fleet management
Downloadable / offline docs: Packages for all platforms
Notes: SELECT pid, name FROM processes WHERE ... changes how you think about endpoint state. The schema is the documentation.

Name: Falco
SDKs & notable repos: CNCF project; syscall-level rule engine with a small rules language; modern eBPF driver
Downloadable / offline docs: Packages, Helm chart, Docker images
Notes: The default open-source runtime threat detector. Rules read like 'spawned process' + 'parent is shell' — readable is why it gets adopted.

Name: Tetragon
SDKs & notable repos: eBPF-based security tracing and enforcement from the Cilium project; policies as Kubernetes CRDs
Downloadable / offline docs: Helm deployment; docs online
Notes: Where Falco detects, Tetragon can enforce — policy applied at the syscall, process blocked in place. Read a TracingPolicy CRD; it is the whole design.

Name: AppArmor
SDKs & notable repos: Path-based LSM; profiles compiled into kernel-enforced policy; the Ubuntu default
Downloadable / offline docs: Userspace tools packaged per distribution
Notes: Easier to adopt than SELinux, weaker at scale. Kubernetes has supported it for years and most people never turn it on — check yours.

Name: SELinux
SDKs & notable repos: Type-enforcement LSM; labels on everything, allow rules between types; userspace tools (semanage, sealert, ausearch)
Downloadable / offline docs: Kernel documentation under Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/; userspace in-repo
Notes: RHEL-family containers are genuinely sandboxed because of it. The learning curve is labels, not rules — draw the type graph first.

Name: Linux Audit (auditd)
SDKs & notable repos: Kernel audit subsystem + userspace (auditd, auditctl, ausearch, aureport)
Downloadable / offline docs: Packaged everywhere; the documentation is the man pages (auditd(8), audit.rules(7)) and your distribution's security guide
Notes: Listed by name because there is no documentation portal to link — and because 'what did that process actually do' is a question auditd answers and everything else infers.

Name: kube-bench
SDKs & notable repos: Implements the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark as runnable Go tests per node role
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; container image; Job manifests
Notes: Run it against any cluster you inherit. The failed checks are a prioritized hardening backlog you did not have to write.

Name: kube-hunter
SDKs & notable repos: External and internal cluster attack-surface scanner; passive and active modes
Downloadable / offline docs: Container image; runs as a pod
Notes: Run it from outside first — what an attacker sees is usually more than the owner expects.

Name: Checkov
SDKs & notable repos: Misconfiguration scanner for Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm and more; policies in Python or YAML
Downloadable / offline docs: pip-installable; pre-commit and CI integrations
Notes: The point is not the scanner — it is that 'public S3 bucket' becomes a failing test before the PR merges.

Name: Prowler
SDKs & notable repos: Multi-cloud posture assessment (AWS/Azure/GCP) implementing CIS and other frameworks; documentation site at docs.prowler.com
Downloadable / offline docs: pip/Docker; runs with read-only credentials
Notes: The open-source answer to a CSPM subscription. The first run on any cloud account is always educational.

Name: Keycloak
SDKs & notable repos: OIDC and SAML identity provider; admin REST API; SPI extensions; themes
Downloadable / offline docs: Container-first deployment; docs per major version
Notes: The default open-source IAM. Standing it up is an afternoon; understanding realms, clients and mappers properly is what interviews probe.

Name: Ory
SDKs & notable repos: Composable identity stack in Go: Kratos (identity), Hydra (OAuth2/OIDC server), Keto (permissions), Oathkeeper (proxy)
Downloadable / offline docs: Docker images; each service standalone
Notes: For when one monolithic IdP is the wrong shape. Hydra alone is the cleanest open-source OAuth2 server to read.

Name: Dex
SDKs & notable repos: Federated OIDC provider — LDAP, GitHub, Google, static passwords in; one OIDC client contract out
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; Helm chart
Notes: The standard 'make Kubernetes authenticate against the corporate IdP' glue. Small enough to read the connectors.

Name: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749)
Downloadable / offline docs: Text/HTML/PDF from https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749
Notes: Read 6749 (framework), 6750 (bearer tokens), 7636 (PKCE) — and then the OAuth Security Best Current Practice, which quietly deprecates half of what the original RFC permits. Authorization-code-with-PKCE is the only flow to default to.

Name: OpenID Connect
Downloadable / offline docs: The OIDC specifications are free on openid.net
Notes: OAuth says 'access the resource'; OIDC adds 'and who is the user' via the ID token. If a login page calls itself OAuth, it is OIDC underneath or it is wrong.

Name: FIDO2 / WebAuthn
SDKs & notable repos: Browser API + CTAP authenticators; server libraries for every platform
Downloadable / offline docs: W3C spec free online
Notes: Phishing-resistant by construction: origin binding kills credential forwarding. The guide is the fastest read; the spec answers the 'actually, how' questions.

Name: libsodium
SDKs & notable repos: Portable fork of NaCl; bindings in every language
Downloadable / offline docs: Full documentation online; source builds everywhere
Notes: If you are choosing between AES and ChaCha20 by hand, you have already failed the API-design test libsodium passed for you. High-level constructs first, primitives never.

Name: OpenSSL
SDKs & notable repos: The openssl CLI (x509, s_client, genpkey); libcrypto/libssl; the providers model since 3.0
Downloadable / offline docs: Man pages; the CLI is on every system you will ever SSH into
Notes: Installed everywhere, misused everywhere. openssl s_client -connect host:443 is still the fastest TLS reality check.

Name: BoringSSL
SDKs & notable repos: Google's OpenSSL fork used by Chrome and Chromium; no versioned releases, no stable API
Downloadable / offline docs: Git checkout; documentation minimal
Notes: googlesource.com rejects some automated clients; loads normally in a browser. Read it to see what a hardened, de-featured crypto library looks like.

Name: RustCrypto
SDKs & notable repos: Pure-Rust crates per algorithm: sha2, aes-gcm, chacha20poly1305, rsa, the elliptic-curve family
Downloadable / offline docs: crates.io; docs.rs per crate
Notes: The interesting engineering is in the audited cores and constant-time discipline. Use argon2 for passwords, not a bare hash — the repos say so; believe them.

Name: Google Tink
SDKs & notable repos: Per-language libraries (Java, C++, Go, Python) with key management as a first-class concept; rotation built into the API
Downloadable / offline docs: Maven/PyPI/npm artifacts
Notes: The library that treats key rotation as a type-system concern. Read the crypto-configuration rationale even if you never ship it.

Name: age
SDKs & notable repos: Simple, modern file encryption; recipients (keys, ssh keys, plugins) compose into one file format; spec on the site
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; spec as Internet-Draft
Notes: What PGP should have been for files: one format, no web of trust, no algorithm negotiation. Use it before you need it.

Name: SOPS
SDKs & notable repos: Encrypts values in YAML/JSON/ENV files while keeping keys readable; AWS/GCP/Azure KMS, age and Vault backends
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; editor plugins
Notes: The pragmatic GitOps secrets answer: secrets live in the repo, encrypted, and diffs stay readable. Mind the rename — it moved from Mozilla to getsops.

Name: Ghidra
SDKs & notable repos: NSA's open RE platform; decompiler for many architectures; scripting in Java and Python; headless analyzer
Downloadable / offline docs: Release binaries include full offline documentation
Notes: The free IDA. Decompiler output plus version tracking makes whole malware families tractable without a commercial license.

Name: radare2
SDKs & notable repos: Unix-style RE toolkit: disassemble, patch, diff, debug, forensics; r2 scripting and pipeability
Downloadable / offline docs: Builds everywhere; the radare2 book is free online
Notes: Steep, idiosyncratic, extremely powerful. Learn aaa, pdf and axt and you can survive; the rest arrives by need.

Name: Cutter
SDKs & notable repos: Qt GUI for rizin (the radare2 fork); decompiler plugins; plugin API
Downloadable / offline docs: Installers and AppImages
Notes: The friendliest entry into binary analysis. Start here; drop to the r2/rz CLI when the GUI gets in the way.

Name: YARA
SDKs & notable repos: Pattern-matching rules for identifying and classifying malware; the de-facto industry rule format; large public rule collections
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; libyara for embedding
Notes: Writing three rules against real samples teaches strings, PE modules and conditions faster than any tutorial. False positives are the actual lesson.

Name: Volatility 3
SDKs & notable repos: Memory forensics framework; symbol tables per kernel build; plugins for process, network and malware analysis
Downloadable / offline docs: pip-installable; framework and plugins in-repo
Notes: RAM never lies about what ran. Running windows.pslist on a memory image you captured yourself is the fastest forensics lesson available.

Name: capa
SDKs & notable repos: Detects capabilities in executables against thousands of rules (capa-rules); Ghidra and IDA plugins
Downloadable / offline docs: Single binary; rules database in-repo
Notes: The polite way to start malware triage: ask capa 'what can this do?' before reversing anything by hand.

Name: Executable formats: ELF & PE
Downloadable / offline docs: Both free online; the System V ABI ELF archives are hosted at refspecs.linuxfoundation.org
Notes: Read both once. Every loader, packer and memory-forensics plugin is an opinion about these two documents, and Ghidra's loaders encode them literally.
